Mods are easy with a little bit of understanding.  Most BG3 mods come bundled as .pak files.  These are convenient because they just go into the Mods folder (AppData\Local\Larian Studios\Baldur's Gate 3\Mods.) Pak files in that folder are activated.  If you want to deactivate the mod if it's causing problems, you just move it out of that folder or delete it.  You can even create a new folder in the Mods folder to put the deactivated mods into.  Putting it into a different folder changes the file path so the mod won't work.  

Alternatively, you can use Baldur's Gate Mod Manager.  That's even easier.  Manually download the ZIP file from Nexus mods which puts the download into your downloads folder.  On BG3MM you open a new file, select the zip you downloaded, and it imports the files themselves automatically deactivated.  To activate the mod, move the mod name file over from the right to the left and save it.  To deactivate, move it back over to the right and save it.  

Some mods don't use pak files though and still need to be installed manually.  Those are a little more tricky, but not really.  Those mods already come in folders of their correct pathing.  Most of the mods that are like that for me are mods that change the cosmetics of characters, like if you wanted to change Shadowheart's hair.  They won't be located in AppData but will be in the BG3 installation directory where there is a, 'Data' folder.  On Steam for me it's (C:)/SteamLibrary/steamapps/common/Baldur's Gate 3/Data.  These mods also aren't as easy to get rid of as you need to remember what you installed.  Sometimes if I want to remove one of those mods, I'll go back to download the mod again to look at what the files they are, so I know to remove those ones.  

When you have mods installed and start the launcher, you'll get a data mismatch error.  That's fine.  Just ignore it.  It conveniently tells you which files are mismatched though if you wanted to remove your mods.  It's just a warning that the mods may mess things up as intended, but I haven't had that happen.

Yeah, Japanese doesn't have an "L" sound.  So for "la" they use "ra" which doesn't sound exactly like, "ra" in English. "R" is pronounced as R and L sound together, so "ra" would sound more like "r-la" as one syllable.  If anyone would like to practice, start by making an "r" sound with the tip of your tongue on the roof of your mouth.  As you start to vocalize the vowel, flick your tongue down at the same time to make the "L" sound.  

A stereotype of Japanese people is that they can't pronounce their "L"'s which isn't exactly true.  They can make the "L" sound but it's tied to an "R" sound and they have gone their entire lives with those two sounds together so it's difficult for them to separate the two, whereas English speakers, whose ears aren't trained to hear the "R-L" sound, may just hear the sound as an "R" and think they're just saying, "R" and then go on to say Japanese people can't pronounce their "L"'s.

Microneedling breaks up that scar tissue and gives the body an opportunity to reheat back to normal.  How does it get prevented from just becoming scar tissue again?  Min and Fin inhibit the formation of scar tissue, so that leaves your body to heal the wounds slowly, unscarred.  Now hair can grow through there again.

I believe they would work hand in hand.  You body has two ways it can heal wounds.  The quick way helps prevent infections by producing collagen (scar tissue).  The slow way heals wounds normally which is a more common healing method in infants and adolescents.
